meta.blurb: Look up from a dark hilltop and you are looking into the past. In fifty short steps, this book follows the story back to the Big Bang and forward to the far future, and says plainly what nobody knows yet.
meta.bible: You: the reader, sitting on a hilltop on a clear night; the book begins and ends there. Universe, Milky Way, Sun, Earth, Moon, Jupiter, Mars, Andromeda: real places. Nicolaus Copernicus (1543, the Sun at the centre), Galileo (1610, four moons of Jupiter), Isaac Newton (late 1600s, Gravity) and Albert Einstein (1915, general Relativity): real scientists, told plainly. Key terms: Light-year, Galaxy, Galaxies, Telescope, Black Hole, Event Horizon, Big Bang, Redshift, Hydrogen, Helium, Carbon, Oxygen, Iron, Calcium, Nuclear Fusion, Microwave, Inflation, Supernova, Red Giant, White Dwarf, Electrons, Protons, Neutrons, Quarks, Quantum, Electromagnetism, String, Dark Matter, Dark Energy, Big Rip, Gravitational Waves, Observable. Facts: the Sun's light takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth; the Milky Way holds at least a hundred billion stars; the universe is about 13.8 billion years old; the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago; the microwave glow dates from about 380,000 years after the beginning; the Sun will swell into a red giant in about five billion years; ordinary matter is about 5 per cent of the universe, dark matter about a quarter and dark energy about two thirds; the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across. Where science is unsure (what came before the Big Bang, inflation, dark matter, dark energy, how life began, the far future), the text says so plainly. Voice and tone: wondering, calm and honest, speaking to you directly, with fresh everyday comparisons (dough and raisins, a cooling cup of tea, a marble in a bowl); no named people other than the historical scientists above.

beats.scene: A person sits on a dark hilltop looking up at the stars
beats.summary: On a clear night on a hilltop, you look up and ask where everything came from.

beats.scene: A beam of sunlight travels across dark space from the Sun to the Earth
beats.summary: Light takes time to travel: sunlight needs about eight minutes to reach us, and a light-year is the distance light covers in a year.

beats.scene: A telescope on a hill points at a faint star
beats.summary: Because light takes time, looking at distant things means looking into the past.

beats.scene: The Sun with eight planets on round paths in a row around it
beats.summary: The Earth is one of eight planets that travel around the Sun, which is our nearest star.

beats.scene: A great spiral of billions of glowing stars seen from far above
beats.summary: The Sun is one of at least a hundred billion stars in a spiral galaxy called the Milky Way.

beats.scene: Thousands of distant galaxies glow as tiny spots in a dark sky
beats.summary: Our galaxy is one of hundreds of billions of galaxies in the part of the universe we can observe.

beats.scene: An old astronomer draws the Sun at the centre of circles on parchment
beats.summary: People once believed the Earth was the centre of everything; in 1543 Copernicus proposed that the Earth moves around the Sun.

beats.scene: Galileo points a small telescope at Jupiter and its four tiny moons
beats.summary: In 1610 Galileo uses a telescope to see moons circling Jupiter, showing that not everything circles the Earth.

beats.scene: A planet follows an oval path around the Sun, held by an invisible pull
beats.summary: Newton showed that gravity, the pull that makes things fall, also keeps the planets in their orbits.

beats.scene: A heavy ball sinks into a stretched blanket while a marble rolls around it
beats.summary: Einstein's later idea: mass bends space and time, and objects follow the curves.

beats.scene: A satellite orbits high above the Earth with a clock on board
beats.summary: Time runs slightly faster high above the Earth than on the ground, and navigation satellites must correct for this.

beats.scene: A huge star collapses into a dark sphere that bends the starlight nearby
beats.summary: A very heavy star can collapse into a black hole, where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.

beats.scene: A dark circle ringed by glowing gas hangs in the black of space
beats.summary: What happens at the very centre of a black hole is unknown, because our theories break down there.

beats.scene: Distant galaxies glow redder as arrows show them moving away from us
beats.summary: In the 1920s astronomers found that other galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther away they are, the faster they go.

beats.scene: Raisins in rising dough drift apart as the dough swells in an oven
beats.summary: Galaxies are not flying through space; space itself is stretching, like dough with raisins in it.

beats.scene: A film strip runs backward as galaxies crowd together into a glowing point
beats.summary: If the universe is expanding, then long ago everything was closer and hotter; about 13.8 billion years ago it was extremely hot and dense.

beats.scene: A grid of lines stretches evenly in every direction with dots spreading apart
beats.summary: The Big Bang was not an explosion in a place; space itself began to expand everywhere at once, so there is no centre.

beats.scene: A glowing speck floats in darkness beside a blank blackboard
beats.summary: Physics can follow the universe back to a tiny fraction of a second, but the very first moment is unknown.

beats.scene: A hot glowing fog of tiny particles fills a dark space
beats.summary: In the first minutes the universe was a hot soup, and the cores of the simplest atoms, hydrogen and helium, formed.

beats.scene: A faint glow fills the whole sky as the first light is set free
beats.summary: After about 380,000 years the universe cooled enough for light to travel freely; that ancient light is still with us as the microwave glow.

beats.scene: The first stars switch on like lamps in a dark fog of gas
beats.summary: After a dark age, gravity pulled gas together and the first stars lit up a few hundred million years after the beginning.

beats.scene: Inside a star, hydrogen cores press together and bright light flows out
beats.summary: Stars shine by joining hydrogen cores into helium, which releases energy.

beats.scene: A star bursts open and scatters glowing clouds of dust into space
beats.summary: Stars build heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron, and scatter them into space when they die.

beats.scene: A child holds out a hand beneath a glowing night sky
beats.summary: Most of the atoms in our bodies, apart from hydrogen, were made in stars, so we are made of star material.

beats.scene: Gas clouds swirl into a great spiral of glowing stars
beats.summary: Gravity gathered gas and stars into galaxies, and some galaxies merged to make larger ones.

beats.scene: A spinning disc of dust and gas circles a young bright Sun
beats.summary: About 4.6 billion years ago a cloud of gas and dust collapsed to form the Sun, and the planets grew from the disc left over.

beats.scene: A young Earth glows red-hot as a huge rock crashes into it
beats.summary: The young Earth was hot, and most scientists think the Moon formed when a body the size of Mars struck it.

beats.scene: Tiny living cells drift in a warm shallow sea beneath a young sky
beats.summary: Life appeared on Earth early, with the oldest signs more than 3.5 billion years old, but how it began is unknown.

beats.scene: A telescope watches a distant star as small planets cross its glow
beats.summary: Thousands of planets have been found around other stars, but whether life exists elsewhere is unknown.

beats.scene: Four arrows of different colours point between atoms, planets and a magnet
beats.summary: All the pushes and pulls in nature come from four forces: gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong and weak nuclear forces.

beats.scene: A tiny dot in a huge empty space with a faint cloud
beats.summary: An atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny core of protons and neutrons and a cloud of electrons around it.

beats.scene: A tiny particle spreads like a wave, then lands as a dot
beats.summary: In the quantum world tiny things act like both waves and particles, and only the chances of each result can be predicted.

beats.scene: A blurred ball inside a tiny box with a ruler and a stopwatch nearby
beats.summary: The uncertainty principle says we cannot know exactly both where a particle is and how it moves; this is part of nature, not a failure of tools.

beats.scene: Two great books, one about stars and one about atoms, will not fit together
beats.summary: General relativity describes the huge and quantum physics describes the tiny, but they do not fit together, and a theory of everything is still sought.

beats.scene: A spinning galaxy with an invisible glowing halo drawn around it
beats.summary: Galaxies spin so fast that their visible matter cannot hold them together, so unseen dark matter seems to add gravity.

beats.scene: Galaxies speed apart faster and faster across a dark, widening space
beats.summary: In the late 1990s astronomers found that the expansion is speeding up, and the unknown cause is called dark energy.

beats.scene: A circle divided into three shares, with one tiny share glowing brightly
beats.summary: Ordinary matter is only about five per cent of the universe; dark matter is about a quarter and dark energy about two thirds.

beats.scene: A great clock face fades into mist before its very first hour
beats.summary: Did time begin with the Big Bang? Nobody knows whether something came before it.

beats.scene: A tiny bright speck swells hugely in a sudden flash of light
beats.summary: Inflation is the idea that the universe grew enormously in a tiny fraction of a second at the start; it is a leading idea, not yet proved.

beats.scene: Faint ripples in the early glow become bright clusters of galaxies over time
beats.summary: Tiny differences in density in the early universe, seen as ripples in the microwave glow, grew into galaxies.

beats.scene: A glowing circle around an observer marks the limit of sight
beats.summary: We can only see the part of the universe whose light has reached us, about 93 billion light-years across; what lies beyond is unknown.

beats.scene: A steaming cup of tea cools on a table beside a spoon
beats.summary: Time seems to run one way: a cooling cup of tea never heats itself up, because disorder tends to increase.

beats.scene: A dry, hot Earth lies under a large red Sun in a pale sky
beats.summary: The Sun is slowly getting brighter, and in perhaps a billion years the Earth will probably be too hot for oceans.

beats.scene: A swollen red giant Sun glows beside a small white dwarf left behind
beats.summary: In about five billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant, then shed its outer layers and shrink to a white dwarf.

beats.scene: A few faint red stars shine in an almost empty dark sky
beats.summary: Over trillions of years the stars will probably run out of fuel, and if dark energy continues, distant galaxies will move out of sight; this is uncertain.

beats.scene: Three paths split from a glowing point, each leading to a different sky
beats.summary: Other endings, such as a collapse or a Big Rip, have been suggested, but present evidence does not favour them.

beats.scene: A radio dish, a space telescope and an underground detector under a night sky
beats.summary: We learn about the universe with telescopes, satellites, particle colliders and detectors of gravitational waves, first caught in 2015.

beats.scene: A scientist crosses out a wrong idea on a board
beats.summary: Science works by guessing, testing and dropping ideas that fail, and it admits what it does not know.

beats.scene: A small figure sits beneath a vast sky holding a glowing lantern
beats.summary: We are tiny in a vast universe, yet we are the part of it that can wonder and understand.

beats.scene: The same hilltop at night, with the traveller smiling up at the stars
beats.summary: Back on the hilltop, the sky is the same, but now you can read some of its story, and many questions remain open.

B1B2: Imagine you are sitting on a hilltop on a clear, dark night. Above you, thousands of stars are shining, and you start to wonder where it all came from.
Light is the fastest thing there is, yet it still needs time to travel. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth, and a light-year is the distance that light travels in one year.
The light from a faraway star left it long ago. When you look at that star, you see how it looked in the past, not how it looks tonight.
Our home, the Earth, is one of eight planets that travel around the Sun. The Sun is a star, and it only looks different from the others because it is so close.
The Sun belongs to a huge family of stars called the Milky Way galaxy. It holds at least a hundred billion stars, and the Sun is just one of them.
For a long time, people did not know that other galaxies existed. Telescopes now show hundreds of billions of galaxies, and each one has its own huge crowd of stars.
For a very long time, most people thought that the Earth stood still at the centre of everything. In 1543, Copernicus published a book that put the Sun at the centre instead.
In 1610, Galileo pointed a small telescope at Jupiter and saw four tiny moons circling it. This showed that not everything in the sky goes around the Earth.
In the 1600s, Isaac Newton showed that one force explains both a falling stone and a moving planet. That force is gravity, the pull between all things that have mass.
In 1915, Albert Einstein gave a new idea of gravity. Heavy things bend space and time around them, and other things follow the curves that result.
Clocks run at slightly different speeds in different places. A clock on a satellite high above the Earth ticks a little faster than one on the ground.
When a very big star runs out of fuel, it can collapse into a black hole. Its gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.
Scientists can describe a black hole from the outside very well. At its centre, however, our best theories stop working, so nobody knows what really happens there.
In the 1920s, astronomers noticed that the light from distant galaxies is stretched toward red. This means that the galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther they are, the faster they go.
Think of raisins in a lump of dough that is rising. As the dough grows, every raisin moves away from all the others, and no raisin is at the centre.
If the universe is growing, then in the past it was smaller. Nearly fourteen billion years ago, everything was packed together in a state that was extremely hot and dense.
Many people imagine the Big Bang as a bomb going off in empty space. In fact, space itself grew everywhere at once, so there is no centre that we can point to.
Scientists can follow the story back to a tiny fraction of the first second. Before that, we do not have a theory that works, so the very first moment is still a mystery.
For the first few minutes, the universe was hotter than the centre of a star. During this time, the cores of the simplest atoms formed, mostly hydrogen and some helium.
After about 380,000 years, the universe became cool enough for light to travel freely. That very old light is still all around us, though it has faded to invisible microwaves.
After the first light faded, the universe was dark for a long time. Gravity slowly pulled clouds of gas together, and the first stars began to shine a few hundred million years later.
A star is a giant ball of gas that is squeezed by its own gravity. Deep inside, hydrogen is turned into helium, and this gives out the energy that makes the star shine.
Over millions of years, stars build heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron. When big stars die in huge explosions, they throw these elements out into space.
Most of the atoms in your body, apart from hydrogen, were made inside stars. In that sense, you are made of stardust, the ashes of stars that died long ago.
Gravity did not only make stars; it also gathered them into galaxies. Over billions of years, small galaxies joined together to make larger ones, and the process still goes on.
About four and a half billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust began to collapse. Most of it formed the Sun, and the planets grew from the flat spinning disc that was left over.
The young Earth was hot and covered with melted rock. Most scientists think that a body about the size of Mars crashed into it, and the Moon formed from the pieces.
The oldest signs of life on Earth are more than three and a half billion years old. How life began, however, is still one of the great unanswered questions of science.
Astronomers have found thousands of planets around other stars. Some of them may be the right size and temperature for life, but so far nobody has found life beyond the Earth.
All the pushes and pulls in nature come from just four basic forces. They are gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong and weak forces that act inside atoms.
An atom has a tiny core, made of protons and neutrons, with light electrons around it. Most of the atom is empty space, and the core is made of even smaller pieces called quarks.
In the world of the very small, particles can behave like waves. Quantum physics cannot say exactly where one will land, only how likely each place is.
There is a limit to what we can know about a tiny particle. The more exactly we measure its position, the less exactly we can know how it is moving.

One theory explains the very big, such as stars and galaxies, and another explains the very small. Each works very well, but they do not fit together, and scientists are still searching for a theory that joins them.
Galaxies spin so fast that the stars we can see should fly apart. Astronomers think that a hidden kind of matter, called dark matter, adds extra gravity to hold them together.
In the late 1990s, astronomers found that the universe is not slowing down as it grows. Instead, its growth is speeding up, and the unknown cause is called dark energy.
Put together, the pieces make a surprising recipe for the universe. Ordinary matter is only about five per cent, dark matter is about a quarter, and dark energy is about two thirds.
Did time itself begin with the Big Bang, or did something come before it? Some scientists think that time began there, while others suspect something existed earlier, and nobody can say for sure.
Many scientists think the young universe grew enormously in a tiny fraction of a second. This idea is called inflation, and it is a leading idea although it is not yet proved.
The glow from the early universe is almost, but not perfectly, smooth. Tiny ripples in it were the seeds of later clumps, and gravity slowly turned them into galaxies.
We can only see the part of the universe from which light has had time to reach us. This observable universe is about 93 billion light-years wide, and what lies beyond it, nobody knows.
A hot cup of tea always cools down, and it never heats itself up again. Physicists say that things naturally move from order to disorder, which gives time a direction.
The Sun has been getting slowly brighter ever since it was born. In a billion years or so, the Earth will probably be too hot for liquid oceans, but that time is far, far away.
In about five billion years, the Sun will swell into a red giant. After that, it will shed its outer layers and shrink to a small, faint star called a white dwarf.
If the expansion keeps speeding up, distant galaxies will slip out of sight. Over trillions of years, the stars will probably use up their fuel, and the universe will grow dark and cold.

Scientists have suggested other possible endings, such as a slow collapse or a final tearing apart of everything. At present, the evidence does not favour these ideas, but new measurements might change that.
We learn about the universe with giant telescopes, satellites and huge machines that smash particles together. In 2015, scientists even detected ripples in space itself, called gravitational waves.
Science does not work by giving us final and certain answers. Instead, scientists make a guess, test it as hard as they can, and drop it if the evidence says it is wrong.
Next to the whole universe, we are very small, and our time here is very short. Yet in us, a part of the universe has learned to look at itself and to ask questions.
Back on the hilltop, the stars look just as they did before. But now you know something of their story, and you know that many questions are still waiting for answers.
C1C2: Imagine that you are sitting on a hilltop on a clear night, far from the lights of any town, with the whole sky laid out above you. Thousands of stars are shining, and the pale band of the Milky Way crosses the darkness like a river of faint light. It is the perfect place to ask the oldest question of all: where did everything come from?

Nothing travels faster than light, but even light needs time to cross the huge spaces between the stars. The glow of the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach the Earth, and astronomers measure the distances of the stars in light-years, a light-year being the distance that light covers in a single year. That is nearly ten million million kilometres, a number so large that it is easier to feel than to imagine.

Because light takes time to arrive, every look into space is also a look into the past. The light that reaches your eyes from a distant star may have set out hundreds or even thousands of years ago, so you see the star as it was, not as it is tonight. The farther we look, the further back in time we see, and that is what lets astronomers study the young universe with their telescopes.

Our home, the Earth, is one of eight planets that travel along nearly circular paths around the Sun, together with their moons and countless smaller rocks and lumps of ice. The Sun is an ordinary star, though it seems quite different from the others only because it is so very close. Compared with the distances between the stars, the whole solar system is little more than a small and crowded neighbourhood.

The Sun belongs to an enormous family of stars called the Milky Way galaxy, a great spinning spiral that holds at least a hundred billion stars. Our own star lies in one of its quiet outer regions, roughly halfway out from the centre. Light itself needs around a hundred thousand years to cross the galaxy from one side to the other.

For many years astronomers thought that the Milky Way might be the whole universe, and it was only in the 1920s that they proved that some faint patches of light were galaxies in their own right. Today we know that there are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the part of space that we can observe. Each one contains vast numbers of stars, so that the total number of stars is far beyond anything that a person could count.

For most of history, people thought that the Earth stood still at the centre of everything, with the Sun, the Moon and the stars turning around it each day. In 1543 the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus published a book that proposed the opposite, placing the Sun at the centre and sending the Earth on a yearly journey around it. The idea met with doubt, but over the next century the evidence gathered steadily in its favour.

In 1610 Galileo turned a small telescope toward the planet Jupiter and discovered four tiny moons circling it, night after night. Here, plainly visible, was a centre of motion that was not the Earth, and the old picture of a sky that turned entirely around us began to look uncertain. Telescopes have been opening the universe to us ever since, each larger one showing more than the last.

In the late 1600s Isaac Newton showed that a single force could explain both a stone falling to the ground and a planet circling the Sun. That force is gravity, the attraction between all things that have mass, which grows weaker as the distance between them grows larger. With a few simple rules, he could predict the motions of the planets, the tides and the paths of comets.

In 1915 Albert Einstein proposed a deeper account of gravity, in which space and time are joined into a single fabric that can bend. A heavy object such as the Sun makes a dip in this fabric, and the planets roll around it, in the way that a marble runs around the inside of a curved bowl. Careful measurements, including the bending of starlight past the Sun, have supported his theory ever since.

Time is not the same everywhere, and clocks tick at slightly different rates depending on gravity and speed. A clock on a satellite runs a little faster than a clock on the ground, and the navigation systems in our phones must correct for this, or they would soon drift off by many kilometres each day. Einstein's strange ideas are therefore quietly at work in everyday life, in every journey that is guided by a satellite.

When a star much heavier than the Sun runs out of fuel, its core can collapse under its own weight into a region called a black hole. The gravity there is so strong that nothing that comes too close, not even light, can ever get out again, and the boundary beyond which there is no return is called the event horizon. Astronomers have found many black holes by watching how they pull on nearby stars and gas.

From the outside, a black hole can be described with great accuracy, and astronomers have even photographed the glowing ring of gas around one. At its very centre, however, our best theories break down and give nonsense answers, and nobody yet knows what really happens there. Honest science often looks like this: a clear edge to what we know, and beyond it a question that is still open.

In the 1920s astronomers discovered that the light from distant galaxies is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum, rather like the way a siren's note drops as the ambulance moves away. This meant that the galaxies were rushing away from us, and the farther away a galaxy was, the faster it was receding. It was one of the most startling discoveries in the history of science, and it changed our picture of the cosmos.

Picture a lump of dough full of raisins, swelling slowly in a warm oven. Every raisin finds itself moving away from every other raisin, and the farther apart two raisins are, the faster the distance between them grows, though none of them is at the centre. In the same way, the galaxies are carried apart because space itself is stretching, and no galaxy occupies a special place.

If we run the film of the universe backward, the galaxies move closer and closer together, and the whole cosmos becomes smaller, denser and hotter. Nearly fourteen billion years ago, this reasoning says, everything we can see was packed into a state of extraordinary heat and density. Astronomers call the beginning of that great expansion the Big Bang, though the name makes it sound rather more violent than it was.

It is tempting to imagine the Big Bang as a bomb exploding at one spot in an empty room, but that picture is misleading. What began to grow was space itself, everywhere at once, so that there is no centre of the expansion and no place that we could point to and say that it happened there. The whole of what we can see was once squeezed into the same small region, and every place was part of it.

Physicists can follow the history of the universe back to a tiny fraction of its first second, using what they know about matter and heat. Closer to the beginning than that, our theories fail, because they cannot yet deal with such extreme conditions, and so the very first instant remains a mystery. We should be wary of anyone who claims to know exactly what happened then.

In the first few minutes, the whole universe was hotter than the centre of the Sun, and it was a glowing soup of tiny particles. As it expanded and cooled, some of those particles joined together to form the cores of the simplest atoms, about three quarters of them hydrogen and nearly all the rest helium by weight. Those proportions, which astronomers can measure in old stars and clouds of gas, agree beautifully with what the theory predicts.

About 380,000 years after the beginning, the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, and light could at last travel across space without being scattered. That ancient light, stretched by the long expansion into invisible microwaves, still arrives from every direction, and it was first detected in the 1960s. A small part of the static on an old analogue television was once this faint glow, a message from the infancy of the universe.

For a long age after that first glow had faded, the universe was dark, with no stars at all, only clouds of gas drifting through the gloom. Gravity slowly gathered the densest clouds into clumps, and some hundreds of millions of years after the beginning the first stars switched on, ending the darkness. Their light began to warm and change the gas around them, and a new age in the history of the cosmos had begun.

A star is a giant ball of gas, squeezed so hard by its own gravity that the centre becomes unimaginably hot and dense. There, hydrogen cores are forced together to make helium, a process called nuclear fusion, and a small amount of matter is turned into the energy that makes the star shine. The Sun has been doing this steadily for more than four billion years, and it has enough hydrogen to carry on for billions more.

As stars age they build heavier and heavier elements in their cores, including the carbon, oxygen and iron that are so common on our planet. When a large star dies in a titanic explosion, it flings these elements far out into space, where they mix with the clouds of gas that will form later stars. Little by little, the universe becomes richer in the raw materials of planets and of living things.

The hydrogen in your body dates from the first minutes of the universe, but nearly all the other atoms, the carbon in your muscles, the calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood, were forged inside stars. Those stars lived and died long before the Sun was born, and their ashes drifted through space until they became part of a new solar system. In a very real sense, you are made of stardust, and so is everyone you have ever met.

Gravity did more than build single stars, for it also drew them, with huge clouds of gas, into the great swirling cities of stars that we call galaxies. Over billions of years small galaxies merged into larger ones, and the process is still going on today, for the Milky Way is slowly swallowing some of its smaller neighbours. In the distant future, it is expected to merge with the neighbouring Andromeda galaxy.

About four and a half billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust, enriched by the ashes of earlier stars, began to collapse under its own gravity. Most of the material fell into the centre to form the Sun, while the rest flattened into a spinning disc in which grains of dust stuck together and grew into rocks, and finally into planets. Our own world is a leftover from that long process of gathering, a small ball of rock built from the ashes of older stars.

The young Earth was a hot and violent place, its surface partly melted by constant impacts from space. Most scientists believe that a body about the size of Mars struck it in a giant collision, and that the debris thrown into orbit gathered together to become the Moon. The theory is widely accepted, though scientists are still debating some of the details, such as what the colliding body was made of.

The oldest traces of life on Earth are more than three and a half billion years old, and they belong to tiny single cells in the ancient seas. Exactly how those first living things arose from lifeless chemicals is still unknown, and it remains one of the great open questions of science. For most of the Earth's history, life consisted almost entirely of tiny and simple forms.

Over the past three decades, astronomers have discovered thousands of planets circling other stars, and some of them lie at a distance from their star where water could in principle remain liquid. Whether life exists on any of these worlds, nobody can yet say, for no living thing has been found anywhere beyond the Earth. The search is one of the most exciting in modern science, and it has barely begun.

Every push and every pull in the universe, from a falling leaf to a spinning galaxy, comes from just four basic forces. Gravity holds planets and stars together, electromagnetism governs light, electricity and chemistry, and the strong and weak nuclear forces act deep inside the cores of atoms. Physicists dream of understanding all four as different faces of a single underlying law.

An atom has a tiny central core made of protons and neutrons, surrounded by a cloud of much lighter electrons, and almost all of its volume is empty space. If the core were the size of a marble, the whole atom would be about a kilometre wide. The protons and neutrons are themselves built from smaller particles called quarks, as far as we know.

At the scale of atoms, the rules of everyday experience no longer apply, and tiny things such as electrons can behave like spread-out waves and like single particles. The theory that describes them, called quantum physics, can calculate only the chances of each possible result, not which result will occur on a given occasion. Strange as this seems, it is one of the most accurate theories ever tested, and it makes modern electronics possible.

Quantum physics sets a firm limit on what can be known about a tiny particle: the more precisely we find out where it is, the less precisely we can know how it is moving. This uncertainty is not a failure of our instruments, for no cleverness in building them could remove it, but a feature of nature itself. It means that, at the smallest scales, the world is fuzzier than our everyday experience suggests.

Our two greatest theories are the general theory of relativity, which describes gravity and the very large, and quantum physics, which describes the very small. Each has passed every test we have devised so far, yet they do not fit together, and in extreme places such as the centre of a black hole or the first instant of the universe, they give conflicting answers. Ideas such as string theory try to unite them, but none has yet been proved.

The stars at the edges of galaxies move so fast that the visible matter alone could not hold them in. Astronomers conclude that galaxies are surrounded by large amounts of unseen matter whose gravity keeps them together, and they call it dark matter because it gives off no light that we can detect. It seems to outweigh ordinary matter by about five to one, yet nobody has found out what it is made of.

Everyone expected the pull of gravity to slow the expansion of the universe, but in the late 1990s astronomers measuring distant exploding stars found that it is actually speeding up. Something is pushing space apart faster and faster, and scientists call it dark energy, although that name is only a label for our ignorance. It is a mystery at the very frontier of physics, and finding out what it is may change science once again.

When all the evidence is added up, the universe turns out to have a surprising recipe. Ordinary matter, the stuff of stars, planets and people, makes up only about five per cent of the total, while dark matter accounts for roughly a quarter and dark energy for about two thirds. Everything we have ever seen with a telescope is therefore a small fraction of what is really there.

Did time itself begin with the Big Bang, or was there something earlier that we cannot yet describe? Some physicists argue that the question of what came before has no meaning, much as asking what lies north of the North Pole has no meaning. Others have proposed bold ideas about earlier universes or about a bounce, but none of these ideas has been confirmed by observation.

Many physicists believe that, in its first tiny fraction of a second, the universe grew by an almost unimaginable factor, from something far smaller than an atom to something far larger. This rapid growth is called inflation, and it would explain several puzzling features of the universe, such as why it looks so alike in every direction. It remains a leading hypothesis rather than a proven fact, and scientists are still looking for ways to test it.

The ancient microwave glow is astonishingly smooth, with temperatures that differ by only about one part in a hundred thousand from place to place. Those tiny ripples mark places where matter was very slightly denser, and over hundreds of millions of years their gravity drew in more and more matter, until the ripples had grown into the galaxies and clusters that we see. The great structures of the cosmos, it seems, began as the faintest of flaws.

Because light takes time to travel, we can see only those regions from which light has had time to reach us since the beginning. This observable universe is about ninety-three billion light-years across, a figure larger than the age of the universe might suggest, because space has been expanding while the light was on its way. Beyond that limit there may be much more, perhaps even endless space, but we have no way to see it and so we can only guess.

A cup of hot tea always cools to the temperature of the room, and it never heats up again by itself, even though the laws of physics for single particles would allow it. The reason is that there are vastly more disordered arrangements of particles than ordered ones, so disorder is overwhelmingly likely to increase, and this gives time its one-way direction. Why the universe began in such an orderly state, however, is still an open question.

The Sun is growing steadily brighter as it ages, and this will change the Earth long before the Sun itself dies. In perhaps a billion years, the heat will probably be enough to boil away the oceans, and the planet will no longer be a comfortable home for anything that lives there. Such a time is so remote that it is useless to worry about it, yet it shows that nothing in the universe lasts for ever.

In about five billion years the Sun will use up the hydrogen in its core and swell into a bloated red giant, swallowing the innermost planets. Finally it will puff off its outer layers into a glowing shell of gas and leave behind a dense, dim remnant called a white dwarf, which will cool slowly for ages. This is a gentle ending, though, since the Sun is not massive enough to explode as a supernova.

If dark energy continues to push space apart as it does today, distant galaxies will eventually move out of sight, leaving each group of nearby galaxies alone in the dark. Over many trillions of years, the stars will probably use up their fuel, and the universe will become a cold, dark and quiet place. This is only the best guess of present-day science, and a better understanding of dark energy could change it entirely.

Other endings have been proposed, including a great collapse in which the universe shrinks again, and a Big Rip in which dark energy grows so strong that it tears apart galaxies, stars and finally atoms. Present measurements do not favour either idea, but they are not yet precise enough to rule them out completely. The honest answer, for now, is that the future of the universe is uncertain.

Everything in this story has been learned by patient observation, with telescopes that collect light, radio waves and X-rays, with satellites that map the ancient glow, and with giant machines that smash particles together. In 2015 detectors on the Earth caught ripples in space itself, called gravitational waves, which were made by two black holes colliding far away. Each new instrument has opened a new window, and each window has shown us something we did not expect.

Science is not a list of final answers but a method for finding out when we are wrong. Scientists propose an explanation, test it as hard as they can against observations, and give it up, however beautiful it may be, if the evidence refuses to agree with it. That is why the story of the universe has changed so often, and why we can trust the parts that have survived every test.

Measured against the size of the universe, a human being is smaller than a grain of dust on a beach, and a human life is shorter than a blink. Yet we are made of atoms that stars forged, and in us a small piece of the universe has become able to look back at the rest and to ask questions about it. We have even found some of the answers, and that may be the most remarkable thing about us.

You are back on the hilltop, and the sky above you has not changed at all, with its thousands of patient stars and its pale river of the Milky Way. Yet you now know that each point of light has a history, that the atoms in your own hands were forged in such fires, and that every answer we have found has opened a deeper question. The story of everything is not finished, and the next chapter may be written by someone who is just now looking up.
